## The Problem With 'Just Do Cardio'

Your clients are googling. And what they're finding is changing their expectations faster than most coaching programs can keep up with.

A fitness coach ranking cardio formats for the Hindustan Times recently put the spotlight on something the industry has quietly known for a while: not all cardio is created equal, and the old hierarchy — run hard, run often — is losing ground to smarter, more accessible options like post-meal walks. Clients are reading this. They're arriving at sessions with questions you need to be ready to answer.

At the same time, Athletech News reports that JetSet Pilates is actively leaning into strength training with new class formats. A Pilates brand adding load-bearing work isn't a gimmick — it's a signal. The line between cardio, strength, and recovery is blurring, and the coaches who thrive will be the ones who blur it intentionally.

## What's Really Happening Here

Two forces are colliding.

First, clients are becoming more modality-literate. They know what zone 2 is. They've heard that a 10-minute walk after dinner does something useful for blood sugar. They're not just showing up and asking you what to do — they're showing up with a framework already half-built, sometimes correctly, sometimes not.

Second, the market is responding. The new Padel Power facility opening in Northampton — reported by the Northampton Chronicle — isn't just adding a gym. It's pairing it with a Pilates studio, and planning soft play on top of that. That's a facility designed around the idea that fitness is a lifestyle stack, not a single discipline. The client who plays padel, then walks to cool down, then hits a Pilates strength class on Thursday isn't an edge case anymore. She's the target market.

If your programming still treats cardio, strength, and mobility as separate silos, you're building for a client who's already moved on.

## What You Should Do This Week

Three concrete moves:

**1. Audit your cardio recommendations.** The Hindustan Times piece is a useful prompt. Where does your current advice land on the spectrum from 'worst to best'? If you're still defaulting to steady-state running as the go-to cardio prescription without context, it's worth revisiting. Low-intensity options like post-meal walks have genuine utility — and they're far more sustainable for most clients. Build them in deliberately, not as a consolation prize for people who 'can't really do cardio.'

**2. Steal the hybrid model.** JetSet Pilates adding strength formats isn't just a class scheduling decision — it's a programming philosophy. Look at your own timetable or client plans. Where can you layer in complementary stimulus? A Pilates client who adds two resistance sessions a week isn't switching disciplines. She's compounding results.

**3. Think ecosystem, not session.** The Padel Power model — sport, Pilates, gym, soft play — is a reminder that retention lives in the whole experience, not the single workout. What does the 48 hours around your session look like for your client? If you're not influencing the walk after dinner or the recovery day movement, someone else's content is.

The coaches reading the same articles as their clients and acting on them first — those are the ones who stay indispensable.
